utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There are two matters I'd like to raise. The first one being that the Chamber invited, as I said, if possible submissions by the parties in relation to where we exactly now stand and what still should be done in the 54 bis application. I don't think we have received anything from the parties yet although there was a related issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The Prosecution made its submissions late last night, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The same is true for the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I should have checked that, but that's done. Then there was -- I a number here, P1265, that is another excerpt, I think, but I'm a bit in doubt about the number. I was just checking. The new selection from this Dutch military --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution will be offering no additional sections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think there were two issues. First is whether you wanted to add anything, and the second is what the section exactly was. And could you remind me about the number, because I thought it was P1265, but I'm a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe that's it, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I look at P1265 in e-court I find a Knin photo presentation rather than an excerpt from ... and there's a surrogate sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe it must be D1265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D, yes that of course makes sense. Let me just check what we have at this moment. Yes, Netherlands army publication. I then understand that the -- I have a 103-page document, and I think part of it was already in evidence. I think it was pages 19 to 22, or something like that. And another selection would be made and Mr. Russo would express his views as to whether to add something. Well, there is not much to be added if all 103 pages are in evidence. Mr. Kehoe, what is your selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My selection, Your Honour, if I can upload it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will hear from you then later this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I can give you the selection and then Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Russo, then you really can answer the question whether you want to add something, yes or no. Having dealt with that matter, I think that we are ready to continue with the witness. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Konings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same procedure as the other days. I would like to remind that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Kehoe will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, we want to go back to where we left off yesterday in talking about P1125 which is Judge Gotovina [sic] order of 1 August 1995 that you referred to - General Gotovina - his order of 1 August 1995. So if we could do that and put that up on the screen. I would like to take to you page 4 of this document just as a reference point before we go to another document, Colonel, so we can put this in context and towards the bottom of that page we are talking about the task of the Split Military District and talking about carrying out a joint offensive going to the last two lines "after the following task": "In a vigorous attack with intense artillery and air support of several axes directed at the main military and political transportation features in the enemy's operational depth." Now you read that to mean when you are talking about in the operational depth, in this instance that would have been the town of Knin, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think certainly that Knin belongs to the enemy's operational depths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let's put this particular reference in context, and I want to show you a document that I'm not certain if you have seen before and reviewed some of the documents but it -- I'm not certain if you have received this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring up D956.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a directive coming from the HV Main Staff dated 26 June 1995. As you can see up in the right-hand corner it deals with Operation Oluja, or Storm. Have you seen this, sir? Let's just page through it and maybe give it a little context. That's page 1 where the Main Staff and in this instance this is signed by General Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite certain about it. I don't think have I seen it, but I cannot give you the full 100 percent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd just like to give you -- apologies. A bit of a feel for this document, Colonel. This is the front page, talking about the military situation. And if we could just page through this and -- as you glance at it, Colonel, please if you want to stop at any point to review it more thoroughly, please say so. Next page as towards the top it gives the status of the enemy. If we can go to the next page. The deployment of forces. Next page is the decisions of the Main Staff. If we can go to the next page. As we can see in point 3 on this page, going over to the next page, we are talking about specific tasks for the Split Military District. Now, this is a normal type of directive coming from a Main Staff being sent down to a commander, such as General Gotovina, on the operational level, is it not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I have seen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And let me just turn your attention to item 7, which is the artillery and rocket support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can just read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Artillery and rocket support shall be provided by 14th and 20th artillery and rocket battalions and an additional 203-millimetre battery. "The support should focus on neutralising the Republika Srpska Army Main Staff and the 7 Corps command post in Knin, the brigade [sic] command posts, concentrations on enemy manpower, armour, and artillery in the area of Knin and Benkovac, including ammunition and fuel depots, while [sic] the supporting the main forces in attack and preventing an enemy counterattack from the direction of Knin, Kastel Zegarski and Benkovac." So looking at this, General Gotovina is being ordered by the Main Staff to uses his artillery and his rockets and direct those artillery and rockets against specific military targets, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And when -- in this instances and you're using these artillery and rocket systems, you are trying to direct them towards specific military targets, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it is -- as described here, yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's take it one step further. I mean, using artillery and rockets I mean you say yes, their Main Staff is doing that because artillery and rocket systems are capable of being directed against specific military targets, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are -- can be directed against any target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, taking this, when this comes down to General Gotovina, he then comes up with the actual plan as to how to executed what the Main Staff wants, knowing that he has been ordered by General Bobetko to direct his artillery against these military objectives that have been listed in paragraph 7 of D956; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that were his thoughts when he received this order. I don't know what he thought, but I assume that he has been reading this order, the complete order, and not only on the artillery support and that he analysed it and that he took from this order the general task that were given him by the -- by the overall staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, okay. You don't have any evidence to conclude that General Gotovina did not follow General Bobetko's order?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I have no -- I assume that he analysed what he received in a way that a military commander does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn your attention back to 1125. And 1125, General, again this is -- this is General Gotovina's order on the 1st of August. I hate to throw these numbers out without putting it in context, but that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 14 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, looking at this item, we again note that it's the use of the various artillery pieces that are at the disposal of the Split Military District that is noted in the initial item. And then we move down to the tasks of the artillery rocket groups: "Groups and organise the TS and TRS-2 along the main attack axes focus on providing the artillery support to the main forces in the offensive operations through powerful strikes against the enemy [sic] front line, command posts, communications centre, artillery firing positions, and by putting the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac under artillery fire. Create conditions to secure the flanks of the units that are involved in the offensive operations along the main axis." Now when we read that, we know that the directive coming from the Main Staff is that it should be directed towards the military targets, objectives that we discussed in D956, the order from the Main Staff. And looking at this particular order, General Gotovina lists the specific items of interest for the Main Staff, command posts, communication centres, artillery positions. Now do you know, sir, whether -- let's put Knin aside, whether command posts, communication centres and artillery firing positions existed in Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't studied the specifics of those cities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You note in your report at page 14 of -- this is paragraph 16, page 14 of P1259, that you were unhappy with the specificity in the order because you say that: "It would give the green light to use the effect of harassment at a maximum by firing randomly into named cities." Have you seen any evidence and we'll talk to Knin at some length have you seen any evidence that the artillery groups under the command -- under General Gotovina in the Split Military District fired randomly at Drvar, Benkovac, Obrovac or Gracac?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen that but did not state that it happened. I said that the point is that by putting this sentence specifically in the order you create the conditions that you allow commanders to do that. Stronger, you order commanders to do that. That's -- that's the point. And the intention may even be worse than the actual fact of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, have you no evidence that it happened?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe the witness answered that the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was a preface to a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I don't know how long you wouldn't to pursue this matter, but it is clear from the report that this witness has no information, at least as far as I understand, about what actually happened. He stopped at the point of where he -- for what it is worth he analysed and looked at the reports and formed the opinion about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My comment with that, Judge, with that -- and I was continuing on with the question, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You know, with that lack of evidence, sir, what we are talking about here is you don't think that this order was written well enough or certainly not according to the doctrine that you were educated in. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is -- the way this specific sentence is phrased here is not only -- not according to our doctrine. It is a sentence that -- and I specifically mean on the sentence: "And by putting the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac and Gracac under artillery fire," that is in our view and I consulted some time ago my colleague who is a legal officer in our organisation is an illegal entry in a document because in the first -- in the complete order of General Gotovina is -- everything is focussed on the use of military means against military targets, and I stated over and over again, I do not have any problem with that because it seems to be a quite normal regular order written according to the standards of the Croatian army which is somewhat different than in NATO but the intention is the same. And if you read the task of the artillery groups, it is in the first part of that tasks it directs the artillery support against enemy front line, absolutely normally. Command post, absolutely normal, and consistent with the orders from the higher staff. Communication centre, artillery firing positions, that's all normal; and that should include the cities of Knin, Drvar as well because if a command post, a military command post is in Knin, then it belongs to that general sentence. And then suddenly out of the blue, as an extra, because it says, "And by putting the towns of Drvar, Knin Benkovac Obrovac and Gracac under artillery fire," I would expect there the sentence, comma, in order to attack command post or specific military targets. There is no explanation where this extra sentence is there. That is the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us analyse what you just said, Colonel, because a fair reading of this quite clearly could be that the artillery groups were ordered to come up with target lists in Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac and Gracac that were directed towards the enemy's front line, command post, communication centres and artillery firing positions. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not putting in that here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not saying it is a perfect order, General. But isn't the interpretation of this order a valid interpretation of the artillery group and in fact what they did was go and look at the enemy front line, the command posts, communication centres and artillery firing positions in Drvar, Knin, Benkovac Obrovac and Gracac --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies. I wasn't sure if he was asking if that is in fact what he did or putting to the witness that is, in fact, what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The objection is therefore not formulated and neither could it stand. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, that is a more than fair interpretation of this order that those particular military objectives were in those cities and that General Gotovina was directing his subordinates to come up with target lists consistent with that for those locations; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, with all due respect I don't think that this is -- I do not have that opinion. I read this in the following way that it is put there as an extra order on top of whatever -- what already has been said in the same sentence command post, communication centre, artillery firing positions because the phrasing is such putting a town under artillery fire without any further explanation, without any reference to the rest of the sentence, that it is and an extra order. And that order, at least in the information that I have, is -- is on no place specified because in order to means that you formulate a clear effect, and I have seen some target lists, we have debated about that in the past days. Those target list didn't gave also no effect, and I think we have to realise when you put out an order that you have to put a town under artillery fire, that you have to be very, very clear in what you mean by that. Because why mentioning that powerful strikes should be done against command post, communication centre, artillery firing positions, and then suddenly say, And by putting ... why not specify it there? I think that's crucial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that -- that you -- you're -- I understand that you disagree with the terminology and I understand what you're saying is that you if you, in the Royal Dutch Army, were doing this, you would have been more specific, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would never use the term put a town under artillery cease-fire. No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you be specific?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's pursuant -- excuse me, General, we're going too fast. And would you be more specific because that would be done pursuant to both your doctrine and your rules of engagement; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has not only to do with doctrine and it has not only to do with specific the rules of engagement. It has do with the way do you your command. It has to do with the fact that once you make such generic phrase in an order, in a mixed, in a complex situation like war is, underlying commanders may understand wrong what is happening here, what is meant from them. What is asked from them. Because specifically when you translate this in a certain way, in this sentence, the order is giving to fire at civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware that prior to this order that the towns of Knin, Benkovac, and Obrovac and Gracac - put Drvar aside - those towns were off limits to HV artillery, pursuant to their rules of engagement. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mine before the Operation Storm started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if those towns were off limits this order is specifically notifying the artillery officers that you're now getting permission to fire on those towns that were previously off limits, firstly; and secondly, that you are to fire on the military objective listed in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, with all respect it does not state it. It does not refer in the whole order that restrictions are taken away and I would expect that to be referred to at least. And it still gives very simple but putting in the word "and by," gives the authority to shell a complete city. It doesn't refer to the previous parts of that sentence because the word "and by putting" is used. I do not understand why such a sentence added to here without any explanation as an extra to the already mentioned command post, communication centre, and artillery firing positions because it introduces in this task a new element, a non-explained element, which again I told before, which has the possibility that artillery is directed against non-military targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm moving to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's take this order and let's go further. As a commander and you as an officer and General Gotovina as an officer, when you give an order you as a senior officer are entitled to presume that your subordinates are going to carry out that order in accordance with the laws of armed conflict; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume I know it for the fact of my own organisation. I cannot look into the head of General Gotovina or Croatian officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the General -- the General accepted military practical that you're familiar with, not only in NATO but throughout the world, is that a senior officer unless he has evidence that his artillery group in this instance that been randomly shelling civilian targets he is allowed to presume that they are operating in accordance with the laws of armed conflict; right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I do not understand why you -- why you create such a misunderstanding or such a very vague order in order to avoid, as I said, misunderstandings and complications in a complex operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't mean to cut you off, sir, but that is not my question, with all due respect. My question is: And if we look back at -- I don't want to repeat the whole thing, on line 14 it's on the screen there: That general accepted military practice, that you're familiar with, not only in NATO but throughout the world. Is that a senior officer unless he has evidence that his artillery group in this instances has been randomly shelling civilian targets he is allowed to presume that they are operating according with the laws of armed conflict. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only answer the question for my own army. I will -- so I will not answer this question. I'm not able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what General Gotovina did because you didn't discuss this in your report. We take this particular order and let's -- if we go two lines down, he notes that in line with the established groups. Do you see that? "The chiefs of artillery in the operations group shall devise artillery plans of use and plans of action each for the representative TS artillery or for their MRL groups the TS or the TRS." So General Gotovina is giving them specific orders to come up with an artillery plan that entails artillery lists tabular textual lists, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the order says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you explain to the Court how this process goes for the artillery group and the mapping, the coming up with the tabular textual coordinates, et cetera, talk to us about that procedure that General Gotovina is ordering?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this in fact means that the underlying artillery groups, and I expect in combination with manoeuvre forces, plan the whole operation, which means they -- they go into the -- the expected enemy, the expected enemy behaviour. They put against that their own courses of action that they have planned to do, and by doing that, they start preparing a list of planned targets, targets that are important that they expect to see on a certain moment in time on a certain location, and they start formulating for each of those targets what they want to do about it in that phase of the operation. And those targets are listed in what we call target lists or a target matrix or whatever it is; and that list specifies the target, the behaviour of the target, the elements of the target. It specifies most and for all the effect that you want to achieve on that target, and it can combine the delivery means that you want to use against it. It is a broad target matrix what you achieve then. And those lists are used as a basis forever the plan target because you also have the planned or prepared targets but you have also unplanned target by opportunity and that are the targets that pop up once are you in the battlefield and you are fighting and something occurs that you didn't -- what you were not able to plan for. So what is said here in line with the established groups, the chiefs of artillery and operating groups shall devise artillery plans of use and plans of action, in itself, is a normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you would expect from this -- by the way, before we go down the process from there. I mean, do you have any evidence or have you been shown any evidence that General Gotovina's subordinates misunderstood this order to mean shell civilian targets or that they had a green light to shell civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the underlying artillery order they in a separate line, not in the text but as a separate order they just repeated that, and in the target list that have I been shown I haven't seen anything back of that. I haven't seen any effects. I only have seen some targets that -- well, we debated that: Hospital, church, medical stations. But when you give the order, shell the city of Knin, you don't need to specify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay putting aside this particular order you haven't shown any other documentation or seen any other documentation that noted there was some green light to attack civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that question has already been asked and answered. I only say that this order could imply that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that. I'm not suggesting that. I only say that this order could imply that. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo wants to intervene then we should give him an opportunity to do so. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just making the objection that that question had been asked already an answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- well, the questions are slightly different now and then but are apparently seeking similar or the same answers, and I earlier indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will move ahead, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and moving ahead means also making progress and leaving behind you what is said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let turn to the document that was -- the Prosecution put in, the map, P1274. Now, sir, this is the type of planning map that you would expect to see that indicates the general areas that you want to put indirect fire into, and I'm talking about the squares; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you focussed on the ones down that are down in the Knin area and during cross we talked about many others. Now within those squares you then would expect individual targets to be identified with the grid coordinates; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This overlay is a part of the whole operational plan or the artillery plan and you have at one hand an overlay and at the other hand that's combined with the target list and the target list gives you the grids.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what we do is we go from the macro, the large plan, and move down the steps to the next item, which is P1271. Putting aside your disagreement of the terminology on church and hospital, this is the type of target list with the grid coordinates you would expect to take from the larger map, down to a table that identifies the targets with grid coordinates; right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception that in this type of list there is nowhere an effect required mentioned. So I cannot really judge what -- what the troops had to achieve here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when you say effect, that's something that your doctrine requires in an order. There is no law of armed conflict that requires an order to have effect?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So just going down to this particular target list this is what you would expect to see. And then if we go to P1272, this is yet a further artillery prep document with those coordinates and the time of actual fire. So, Colonel, going back to P1125, page 14, towards the bottom of the page, from the evidence that you saw, in fact General Gotovina's subordinates did in fact follow his order and the chiefs of artillery devised artillery plannings and use and plans of action for each of their respective units or the artillery groups; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object because the question is based on the assumption that what he has been shown the map and the two target lists were drawn up by the chiefs of artillery. I don't think that has been put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, Mr. Kehoe, what exactly are you seeking? Are you seeking the witness to interpreter this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of course, [Overlapping speakers] ... that given what he has been shown that he can conclude that General Gotovina's subordinates followed his orders, came up with the artillery plan with a map, tabular textual sheets that have grid coordinate, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether at least it was reported to him what they done and that whether this witness agrees that this was in line with the order given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you answer the question. If you need more time to read it, tell us. If not, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything you showed me, as far as my opinion is, my judgement of the operational order is in line with the order with the exception of any logic explanation of the sentence, and by putting the towns of Knin under artillery fire. Because the task of the artillery group is clearly stated, support main forces in offensive operations through powerful strikes against the enemy front line, command post, communication centres, artillery positions. For that purpose, that is it clear enough because they are all military targets. That is clear enough. For all that purpose, target lists have been build, plans have been made, maps have been drawn. That's all very logic. But those plans that I have been shown, those artillery target lists that I have been shown do not reflect the point by putting the towns of Drvar, Knin under artillery fire. I think that is an extra, understand necessary order that is given in this and is not reflected in the points that you showed me. That is my opinion, whatever you think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So let's go to P64 for our final document on this score. Once again, looking at Colonel Hjertnes's conclusions that the -- the general shelling was concentrated against military objectives and if we look back -- and this is just for Knin. And if we look back at the order, the order says to hit command posts, communication centres, artillery positions. What in fact happened in Knin was that military objectives, pursuant to this order, command posts, communication centres, and artillery positions, were in fact hit by the HV and according to General Hjertnes they were all concentrated -- not all. They were concentrated around those targets; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I object to this question because the P64 clearly doesn't indicate and Hjertnes is not indicating that command posts, communication centres, or artillery positions were hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you're asking again, again to the witness what happened. And I already tried to assist you in rephrasing your last question because this witness apparently has no personal observation. He can read the documents as we can do. And then, of course, you could ask him whether this document is an indication for a report that is in line with. That's something which could be understood. But you ask him again and again, Isn't this what happened? He apparently doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you phrase your questions correctly, you will certainly avoid any objections by Mr. Russo and, of course, the point is perfectly clear what keeps you and Mr. Konings divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That point is perfectly clear. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand and if I ask one last question, I will sit down and you won't hear from for the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what I'm aiming ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand I'm just being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and I'm responding with just a similar smile on my face as I see on yours. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General -- Colonel, apologies. You can be a General, I believe you. Just promoted you.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, isn't paragraph 2 in P64 an indication that when they were firing on Knin, the firing was on command posts, communication centres, artillery positions, such as was ordered by General Gotovina in P1125. Isn't that an indication of that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is it only an indication that the fire was concentrated against military objectives. I do not know which objectives. I really don't know, and it also says that there is damage caused to civilian establishments. And I would clearly like to disconnect this -- what happened in practice, with the intention that I read in the order of General Gotovina with that specific sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I just have one moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And one last question, Colonel. Your knowledge concerning General Gotovina's intentions in these regards are strictly what you read or what you have been provided by the OTP. You don't have any other information on that, do you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you very much. You have been very patient with my questions, and I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. No cross-examination by the Cermak Defence. Mr. Kuzmanovic for the Markac Defence. Mr. Konings, Mr. Kuzmanovic is counsel for Mr. Markac, and he'll now cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Konings.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, it's fair is it not to state that in the reports that you were provided there is no opinion critical of, or even discussion of, or an awareness of the Ministry of Interior special police and their use of artillery in Operation Storm; that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who, if anyone, controlled the use of artillery for the Ministry of Interior special police in its axis of attack?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you even aware that the Ministry of Interior special police had artillery at its disposal in its axis of attack?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I concentrated fully on those aspects that we discussed before, the three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's fair to state that the Office of the Prosecutor in this case never spoke to you about any specific issues relating to the use of artillery in Operation Storm by the special police.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can recall now, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you -- did the Office of the Prosecutor speak with you at any point in time about the testimony of a gentleman by the name of Josip Turkalj? Does that name ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the moment, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's fair to say that you don't flow who Josip Turkalj is; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no include.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Office of the Prosecutor at any point in time discuss with you the testimony of a gentleman by the name of Mile Sovilj?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And again it's fair to say that are you unaware of who Mile Sovilj is; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fair to state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your report made a fairly long analysis regarding artillery use in Knin. There is no analysis in your report of the use of artillery in Gracac, Obrovac, or Benkovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: As a result, you do not know whether or not there were any civilian casualties as the result of artillery use in Gracac, Obrovac, or Benkovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were not aware of what collateral damage occurred, if any, as the result of the use of artillery in Gracac, Obrovac, or Benkovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At no point in time during the course of the Operation Storm did the military of the ARSK or their civilian authorities proclaim any of the cities in Sector South, in particular, to be a free or open city; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been reading such a text in any of the documents that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Other than in Knin, did the Office of the Prosecutor make you aware of any military targets in places like Gracac, Benkovac, or Otocac?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was some discussion regarding Exhibit P1273, and for purposes of my question, we don't need to pull that. If you can recall, Colonel, that was the map of Poskok 93 with a list of targets and there was some discussion regarding some of those targets using a word "stacionar," which in some instances was interpreted as a medical station. Do you remember that discussion in your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like the registrar to please pull up 1D65-0257.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This particular document is dated the 29th of July, 1995. And it isn't specifically related to artillery, but if you will see in paragraph 3, on the B/C/S version of the document, there is the use of the word "stacionar," and it is translated in this particular document to mean stationary facility and not medical facility. Were you given any information at all, Colonel, about whether or not "stacionar" meant anything other than medical facility?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall, we have never debated about the word "stacionar." I have been shown the target list where the word medical station came on, and I only have one explanation for the word medical station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. For example in paragraph 3 of this order, and I will read it. It says: "After the handover of positions, the POB shall withdraw to the Sveti Filip i Jakov stationary combatant accomodation with the task of conducting preparations for occupying the pp." In this particular context at least stationary combatant accommodation is a place in which troops are quartered; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're reading apparently from a translation which is not the same as I have on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You apparently are reading from a translation which is not the same as I have on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will read it from the screen, Your Honour, if it's -- I have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially because there is just one word that you read, which might be relevant in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the word is in my document, in my hard copy different from the document on the screen, you're correct, Your Honour. I will read from the screen. "After the handover of positions the POB shall withdraw to the Sveti Filip i Jakov stationary facility with the task of conducting preparations for occupying the pp." And I will get back to my previous question, Colonel. At least in this particular order, "stacionar" is not referenced as a medical facility?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apparently it says here stationary facility which can mean well, a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit D1269 is admitted into evidence. I immediately add to that, Mr. Kuzmanovic, that resolving an issue of interpretation but putting another document for which also exists apparently, two different translations might add to the confusion, rather than to resolve it. What I would very much like to know, as a matter of fact, I take it that Saint Filip and Jakov I think that's -- SV stands for saint, but I'm not quite sure about that, would refer to an existing facility. I don't expect them to invent new names. Now, what I, of course, would like to know is what the facility was apparently in this area which was known by the name Saint Filip and Jakov rather than to further focus on confusing translation issues. I don't know whether you come to that or not. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess the whole purpose of using this particular item was just to show the Court there are multiple meanings to the word -- for the use of the word "stacionar. "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if Saint Filip and Jakov was a medical facility. I don't know. I've got no idea what they did there, whether they were baking break or whether -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a city. It's a city in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I follow you now. I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because in the translation it says the Saint Filip and Jakov stationary. I don't know whether that was a name of a village or of a stationary and then of course what stationary was referred to in this document is at least from the mere reading of it not clear. Apparently a stationary of whatever kind, now I understand within this village. It -- the only thing it -- it makes it more complex and not to blame you for making matters that are complex showing that they are complex; but I think I invited the parties to see whether there was any better linguistic approach but a very practical approach could help as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We could do that, Your Honour, and we haven't had the chance to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for the interruption. Mr. Russo and I, as a matter of fact this morning, talked that we need to resolve that issue as soon as possible. I do want to state, however, what with respect to your asking what does stationary facility mean, the -- in the context of Sveti, Saint Filip and Jakov, we'll certainly look into that for you. However it is just our position that it just means in a military context any fixed, hard facility which could mean anything it could mean a school, it could mean a house, it could mean ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's the issue whether it has the medical connotation necessarily or not; I think that's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, but -- from our perspective, Judge, obviously in someplace, somewhere it could have meant a specific medical facility that was being used for a military purpose, a fixed facility. What I'm saying is it's a general term that can mean any facility that is fixed. So here we could find out what was there in that particular village but we would have to do it on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because Mr. Russo has presented us with a dictionary which gives a more specific meaning. Whether or not that is a good dictionary or not is still to be seen. That, of course, keeps you apart whether it is a very general term or whether it has a specific connotation, medical facility. And I don't know Saint Filip and Jakov, whether it brings up any further or whether it throws us further back is still to be seen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you have no evidence or you have not received any evidence any way with regard to whether medical stations were actually hit by artillery in -- in Operation Storm; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your CV is P1258 and I just have a general question about your background, Colonel. At least from my interpretation from the CV it is silent whether have you commanded a field artillery unit in combat. Can you tell us whether you did so or whether you did not? And maybe I misread the CV. Have you ever commanded a field artillery unit in combat?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Has the Office of the Prosecutor ever given you any estimation what the amount of civilian casualties were in any of the cities or villages during Operation Storm as a result of artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We might have touched on some figures. But I cannot recall that now, it's apparently too long ago. I don't know that, so the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At least none of that is contained in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not contained in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said you were in Sarajevo for a considerable period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been in -- stationed in Sarajevo for nearly seven month, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: From when to when?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April 1995 up to the end of October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So during the course of Operation Storm, you were actually in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was actually in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Russo, any need to re-examination the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel, just to address one of the last questions you got Mr. Kuzmanovic asked you if you had ever commanded an artillery unit in combat. Can you tell the Chamber whether the laws of armed conflict as you understand them, and as you were educated in them, whether they apply the same in combat situations and in non-combat situations?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on how you describe the word combat. I think laws of armed conflict are -- are in -- in application throughout any kind of conflict, and currently we don't make any difference anymore between a combat operation or a peace support operation. We talk about the involvement of military forces inside any operation in a conflict and as far as my knowledge goes, the application of violence the application of military means is subject to the laws of armed conflict, no matter you talk about combat yes or no because the definition, the description of combat is the application of military violence against a responsive enemy. That's what we describe on combat. So combat can occur inside a peace support situation. It is not necessarily that we talk about a state to state to conflict in which large armies are combatting each other. Combat also occurs in an irregular situation, like in Afghanistan, where what we have depicted to be counterinsurgency. So I think that -- that all is applicable -- to all the situations the laws of armed conflict is applicable with my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Colonel, you were asked some questions by Mr. Kehoe regarding the military advantage of destroying enemy cohesion by means of fear, panic, shock, and surprise. If you recall that, can you tell the Chamber whether artillery is the only means by which one can achieve these effects against an enemy?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, definitely not. There are much more means available.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Would you mind giving the Chamber just an example or two of what else can be done, other than the use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every weapon system that you have in your inventory that can range from the use of small-arms up to the use of close air support or even larger -- the use of larger air assets, like bombing planes, everything have you in between, the use of lethal means will cause panic or chaos and, of course, have you a whole variety of what we try to summarise under the word information operations where you can use psychological warfare or where you can try to use everything from the non-lethal means that have you available to cause panic, to cause fear, you can threat [sic] people. If people are sensitive for that, you don't need to use your weapons. If you threat people that you will do such, such and such when you come somewhere, people might panic already by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also shown some evidence about the use of railroads by the ARSK to move ammunition sometime between the end of July and the 5th of August, 1995. None of this evidence included any reference to the ammunition being actually in Knin itself or being moved through the town of Knin itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... leading nature of this question, Your Honour, if he wants to go into a particular document, that's fine, but a speech by the counsel is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, would you please reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, in asking about the use of the railroads, Mr. Kehoe asked you the following, and this occurred at 14684, line 2, to 14688 line 7, this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "Now if in fact, Colonel, the ARSK was using these railway lines to move ammunition and if in fact there was some activity in these railway lines on the 4th, you would agree with me that the HV could achieve a significant military advantage by attacking those rail lines and preventing the ARSK from moving any of this ammunition. Isn't that right?" Your answer was to that that, yes, that was right. What I'd like to ask you, Colonel, is if the HV could have used artillery to attack the rail lines at choke points outside of Knin, which were not in the direct environment of civilians why would it be reasonable in your opinion for them to choose instead to shell the main railway station and railway yards inside Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the background of the choice they made to -- to shell the main railway station and the reasons that were behind that, but I look to it in the following way, is that when you try to destroy or stop a -- an ammunition convoy on the train, first of all, you have to realise that when do you that, you might cause a lot of devastation when a train like such depending on the amount of ammunition is in there blows up, and that happens inside a civilian-populated area you will have a major disaster. That's the first thing you have to realise. Secondly, when you choose -- no. When you decide to that on a major railway station, you might destroy a significant part of that railway station, including tracks, including infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we're moving away from what the question was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Kehoe whether -- if railway lines are used for transportation of ammunition, whether the HV could achieve a significant military advantage by attacking those rail lines and preventing the ARSK from moving this ammunition. Now, what Mr. Russo asks you is would it be reasonable to attack the rail lines in a city or would it be more reasonable to do it outside the city, and you are introducing new elements such as trains exploding and that appears not to be the focus of the question. Please proceed -- could you please focus your answer on that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then the answer is simple, I would do that outside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And likewise with the Senjak barracks Mr. Kehoe showed you some evidence that the ARSK had plans to move quartermaster materiel from this location and told you that this was the main logistics supply centre for the 7th Krajina Corps. This was at transcript pages 14677, line 23, to 14680, line 10. Now again, Colonel, if the ARSK could have used artillery to attack logistic supply convoys in an area outside of Knin, which did not endanger civilians, would it be reasonable in your opinion for them to choose instead to fire in the city or outside the city?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, your question is certainly confusing, because the questions put by Mr. Kehoe was an attack to a fixed facility, isn't it? And now you are introducing a new element that is convoys, which are moving --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe the evidence that Mr. Kehoe presented was the destruction of trucks inside the Senjak barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what he introduced was a report in which it was said that three trucks were demolished but in such a way that it did not suggest, and I'm just talking from the top of my head, it said three trucks were destroyed but whether that was part of it, consequence, whether it was an introduction to whether the destruction of these trucks would have made it more difficult to perform the functions that was at least rather unclear for me from that document. So I'm -- I have some difficulties in putting questions on attacking convoys to say isn't that -- if you are talking about the function of supply, which is you have your supplies somewhere, then you move them to a place where they are needed and what would be the best -- but it's now just as if you say, Do it outside the city, but then, of course, you would have to wait until they start moving, isn't it? And if the trucks are destroyed it might well be that there is no ability to move them anymore. So it's a rather complex matter, and if you want to deal with the matter with the witness, fine, as far as I'm concerned. But then let's clearly analyse on the basis of the documents what we exactly see, what the question is, what the -- apparently what you're hinting at alternative options, what they exactly are and not mix everything up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel, what would be the military advantage in attacking a logistics supply base in any event? What's the military advantage to be gained from attacks logistics supply?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logistics supply form the basis for -- for an operation, so depending on the role of a specific logistical supply base, and the amount of supplies that troop in the field have available, that can -- attacking a logistical supply base can have -- can mean a significant military advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like you to describe what -- how you achieve that. If the supplies just stay in the logistics facility and they are not moved out to anyone on the front line or anywhere what advantage is there in attacking that facility?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in itself, then there is no direct advantage to be achieved in attacking that -- that logistical base. And then various factors come into the decision-making process whether to do that, yes or no. You can anticipate on what you expect that that logistical base will do in the future and take nevertheless the decision that you want to destroy it. That's very hard to give any exact meaning about without knowing any further specifics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're using the word nevertheless. Let me try to see whether I can understand. I have a logistical supply base that I have to provide the units wherever they are with whatever is in this supply base. Now wouldn't that save a lot of efforts to destroy the supply bases rather to wait until one truck is moving to the north, you have to hit it when it's moving; another truck is going to the south, have you to hit it when it's moving; then the next day new trucks come in and start transporting. I mean, merely from a point of view of efficiency. If you paralyse the supply system as a whole, you don't have to attack five or ten or 20 trucks trying to distribute the supplies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on the function of that specific logistical base, Your Honour. If that is the only logistical base in the -- for an operation of an army, then you are absolutely right. But you can have -- in most times you have situation that logistical bases are split up and that each subunit has its own smaller supply area and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is then fed by the main supply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. But so if you dry up that main supply area, but there are also situations that -- from a central airport, the smaller supply areas are -- are supplied, and then the convoys are coming in. What you see in Afghanistan now is that convoys are the Achilles' heel not the supply areas but convoys are the Achilles' heel in bringing stuff from Pakistan up to Afghanistan. So it is both. I fully agree with you if you have a large supply base. You can take that out for several weeks then you will hamper the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We were fed with evidence that it was the main supply bases now. I can imagine that -- I try to understand what the word quartermaster exactly meant. But from what I understand but please correct me if I'm wrong. He can take care of the military uniforms and the socks to be resupplied but also ammunition. I mean, main supply, of course, is a rather generic term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I still then do not know whether it is about socks, whether it's about food, whether it's about ammunition, whether it's about spare parts for vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I don't think that is something that we can come to agreement on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, I think that it is the main supply depot for everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's not to say that they weren't -- some of their locations up near the front that the Colonel was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only for you to know that in order to fully understand the issue, it -- it might assist the Chamber in knowing what was supplied from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kehoe also asked you about the St. Ante monastery where according to the facts you were asked to assume the headquarters of the special police forces were located and this was at transcript pages -- page 14659, lines 18 to 22. utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it will not change my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel, you were asked a number of questions yesterday regarding the military advantage of knocking out communications systems and communications centres. And I'd just like to ask you, whether artillery is the only means by which one can disable or disrupt the communications systems of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Artillery is definitely not the only means.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And let's deal first with radio communications. Can you give the Chamber some examples of how else one might disrupt or disable radio communications of an enemy.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other possibilities are the usage of other lethal means that you have available, like depending on the value of that specific communication system or station the use of aircraft with special -- with guided missiles available, or you can also use non-lethal means I mean by that germing or electronic war fare.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Would destroying the radio relay stations of an enemy's radio communication system would that knock out their long-range radio communications capabilities?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be specific in that. It depends on how the system is laid out. If in the case that this is the only -- if there is only one long-range radio relay system, if you knock that out, you will bring down the whole system.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And with respect to land line communication systems -- first of all how can you use artillery to disrupt a land line communication system?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As artillery has the capacity to destroy things or to neutralise things, and if you are -- if have you available the information about how the land lines are constructed and laid out in the terrain or concentrated in a certain area, for example in a building then in itself artillery can be one of the choices to try to take that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Are there means other than artillery that you could use to disable or disrupt land line communication systems?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that every mean in your inventory is one, is one possibility. You can use precision strike with aircraft to take out a the concentration point of land lines, provided they are military. You can send in a Special Forces team to destroy a very important crossing point of land lines. So there are various possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
