utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: I have some questions for you. As the first -- based on two requisites you know military doctrine its application of principle of proportionality and military necessity. Could you please explain competence of principle proportionality in military, sense in military doctrine but in very short way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're reading the transcript, and I think that the transcript is not complete on what you said. I think, Judge Kinis, that you invited the witness to explain briefly in the military sense, the military sense, the military doctrine, the principle of proportionality to start with.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That principle does mean that you if you are forced to apply military violence that you do that in such a way that it is in accordance with the effect that you want to achieve. That means that said in other words that you have the intention to use as less violence as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: It is just only one indication?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the idea that we use in describing shortly proportionality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 52 -- Article 52 on paragraph 2 from Geneva Convention protocol, second protocol -- first protocol of Geneva Convention which the times, what is a military target mentions that it should be justified if there is an first place by military necessity. Could you please explain whether between terms military necessity and proportionality is possible to put equality?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you take a military target, if you have defined that a target is a military target, even then, you have to take into account the principle of proportionality, even then you have to take into account, for example, in your targeting process, the best means to achieve the effect that you want, and you can even consider in killing as much enemy soldiers as you like; but have you another option, is to try to take them as -- as prisoners of war and have various options in between, and that depends on the overall effect that you want to achieve with an operation and from there, I think you look what is proportionate to achieve your end state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But I would like ask you what is your opinion, what is competence of military necessity in this particular case. If attacking force wants to assess -- do assessment for military necessity what kind of competence they should take into account.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, military necessity is linked to, first of all, to every target in itself, what does that target bring to the whole of the operation of an enemy, and once you have designated that from there you build the picture how the combination of those military targets together will bring that -- the end state that you want to achieve in an operation. Because an operation may be used as a -- may be aimed at total go destruction of an enemy but an operation may also be aimed at separating two warring factions so everything you do in combatting military targets has to do with the goal you want to achieve and that is not something that is done purely by military. That is also something, especially something that is directed to you by -- well, your political superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with concept of critical information infrastructure, the determination of critical information infrastructure of the state.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the term. I'm not really familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: It means that there should be included all objects which are very important for state security.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: My question is would be possible to get anticipated military advantage without attacking objects of critical information infrastructure like post, telegraph, radio, communications, and et cetera.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well that depends on how the critical information infrastructure is connected to the military structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: I mean in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in relation to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apparently in this case, several of the critical information infrastructures were used in one way or the other by the military. And some of these critical infrastructures had a real critical role because apparently they were the only one in the region that provided communication or else, and then you come into a situation that -- that this is, of course, real critical to take it out, yes or no; and especially if that is a combination of military personnel and materiel, and civilian personnel and materiel and civilian personnel and materiel involved well, then this is a very hard solution to make or a very hard decision to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But based on this information that you got during -- during this court hearing, and based on this reviewing of documents what would be your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I look to the information that was given to me by the OTP, then I can say that -- that I'll -- I'll keep to my -- my conclusions that I made in my report and my addendum. During the discussions of the past days, various scenarios were described to me by -- by the Defence counsel and every scenario was a different one, and once a scenario changes all the factors in such a scenario or operation changes, and have you to -- that's one thing that in a military operation is very important that a commander and his staff analyse the operation continuously and take into account all new information that you have. That's something I tried to do during the past days as well, and if suddenly the situation changes from there is hardly anybody in the barracks or in a location, towards there are -- there is an complete brigade in that location, well, that changes the whole analysis, and due to the -- to the sometimes the lack of information that I did not have, or that was not given to me, then it's coming very close to impossible to say something very -- very specific about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: It means that you cannot state direct conclusion whether it is possible or not.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say a direct conclusion no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Okay. Based on documents what you reviewed, could you draw conclusion that operation, this artillery attack to Knin, creates collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, as we said, I have not been there, so I don't know that. I -- I -- and from -- given from the information the very scarce information about the real results, I can come to the conclusion that there was collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And could you please specify something about this?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot. And that's the point in that. We were reading that UNMO report, where it stated that civilian property was hit and from that I conclude there must have been some collateral damage but we also said that, and I agreed with that, that there is no specific mention about that and I have no information about that. So everything beyond I say now from my side will be speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, I have one question for you. When I was listening to the sound on the video-clips, I thought, but I'm not experienced at all in that area, I thought that I heard different types of sounds, some of them being explosions but I think in the first portion I also hard a kind of whistling sound rather than explosions. Could you assist me in, first of all, whether I made this distinction by listening well, whether you heard the same; and, second, how I should interpret these different sounds. I heard the whistling sound only once but I might not have been focussed enough.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, I think that you came to a correct conclusion that there were different sounds and that is possible through the fact that different calibres might have been used or different types of weapon systems might have been used. I give me -- maybe I can give you an example, that in the -- in the -- in the war in Vietnam, US forward observers specialised in sounds because they could not see the point of impact of a projectile into the jungle so they specialised in the sound of the exploding projectile and that is a possibility; and I must say that I learned that in Sarajevo as well, in distinguishing between 81, 120 and 152 or 155 or rocket systems that is very well possible. And you don't need to be trained for that to hear the difference. The whistling sound that you heard is -- means that was an artillery projectile because artillery projectiles when fired and when they pass you, you hear that. You may hear that sound, not in all cases. Depends on where you are in -- in comparison with the projectile trajectory. But normally that means it is an artillery projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I then have to understand that where I heard the whistling sounds that it must have been a projectile which passed close enough to the microphone that was used so as to hear it pass rather than to hear it explode from a distance, where it may have not passed -- where the trajectory may not have passed the area but where the microphone was because I heard it only, as I said, once but -- I'm not sure whether you heard that more.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard some more because I have seen a somewhat longer part of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The part played. Everything else --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part played. I know, I think I heard two or three times the same noise. But normally it come through the fact that the projectile is passing roughly above you. When it is passing on the side of you, you might not hear that. So that means that it is fired somewhere behind you, it's passing on top you, and it will explode somewhere in the area before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it does not in any way indicate a different type of weapon or it could be all artillery fire could create such a whistling sound and if it would pass by other trajectory you might not hear that whistling sounds.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing you hear with a mortar projectile you hear a similar sound but that is very close before impact. There is then only a split second when you hear such a sound when a mortar is used and immediately afterwards you hear the impact and you have to be quite close otherwise you don't hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. As I said before, I would give you an opportunity to add anything and I'm not inviting you to repeat anything, but to add anything to your testimony before I give a final opportunity to the Defence to -- to ask further questions, triggered by the re-examination and the questions by the Bench. Is there anything that you'd like to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, everything has been said, so I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any need to put further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one question. The whistling that Judge Orie ask you about that whistling on an artillery fire would be whistling either outgoing or incoming, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that. Distinction is hard to make. You can connect that whistling to either its incoming or outgoing when you are able to hear the -- the actual fires of the Howitzer. Otherwise, it is very hard to define where it coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Once against, thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, there are no further questions for you. I suggest to the parties that any further submissions or any further argument to the extent needed on the question of admission of 1259 up to and including 1262 an issue that P1259 that can be dealt with in the absence of the witness. Then, Mr. Konings, I would like to thank you very much for coming, usually I add to that a long way to The Hague, but that might not be true for you. But for coming to this Court and for considerable time having answered all the questions that were put to you by Prosecution, Defence, and by the Bench. And this concludes your testimony. You are excused. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we deal with a few procedural matters, I'd first like to pay attention to the more general question on how will you -- we will use the remaining time this week. Is my understanding correct, Mr. Russo, or Mr. Waespi, or Mr. Hedaraly, that there's one more witness to be called this week, without protective measures, which would be Mr. Marker-Hansen. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He was scheduled for one half another in chief, as a 92 ter witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. In the 92 ter submission we had provided a revised estimate of two and a half hours, but I am hopeful that examination will be concluded within a session or a little more than a session, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm asking the Defence what the estimates are at this very moment in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would estimate at most three-hours from us, probably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That makes three sessions all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at least one hour from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That take it as a rough figure that makes four sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would say at least three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which makes it six sessions. The reason why I'm explore is the following: We have a few relatively simple procedural matters we could deal with today. The Chamber is a bit surprised by the efficiency in relation to the last witness, to the extent that, on the basis of the estimates, we expected that we would finish this witness by today. I had planned to prepare fully for the pending issues, MFI list, et cetera tomorrow and then deal with it after we finished this witness. Now we have some time left. I'm not fully prepared. Other hand, of course, the Chamber would like to avoid that the next witness would have to stay over the weekend because we are running out of time. Now, six sessions is two hearings. We have as a matter of fact, nine sessions because we are scheduled Thursday, half a day, and Friday, the whole of the day. Can I be confident that if the MFI list will not take more than two sessions, I don't know exactly how much time it will take, that we would nevertheless could conclude this witness if he would start on Thursday because my calculation now is six sessions for the next witness and that means that two or three sessions would remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the only thing that I would like to inform the Court is that the witness did arrange a schedule to be able to testify Thursday and Friday but he must leave at the end of the day on Friday. I would suggest although we had expressed a preference earlier to have the MFI session at the conclusion of this witness's testimony, would prefer to call the witness on Thursday morning to ensure that he is done and deal with the MFI in the last hearing scheduled on Friday afternoon, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I asked for the estimates in order to make a calculation on whether we could do both. And I do see your point, Mr. Hedaraly. The Chamber will consider it. But I would urge the parties that where we have an estimate of six sessions for the witness, and that my estimate for the MFI session would not go beyond two sessions, and hopefully within one session, that we would deal with both the issues, that is, the testimony of the next witness and the housekeeping matters Thursday and Friday. It, at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The information by the parties leads the Chamber to decide that we'll not try in an unprepared way to deal with major portions of MFI list/housekeeping sessions today and that we will try to do it all on Thursday and Friday. Then I have a few -- yes, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There is one procedural matter that we'd like to address. We can do it later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few if it is not dealt with by me, then, of course, you're invited to raise the issue. There was a request by the Cermak Defence to go beyond the word limit on admission of a 300-page document, objections against admission, at least I take it that it will be objections. I do understand that the OTP does not oppose the limited extension of the word limit because the issue was 3.000 or 3900. Now, is that -- 3900 is that what you really need, I mean if we would say 4.000, would that meet your request.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We have drafted the motion, Your Honour, as Your Honour will be aware that the deadline is tomorrow. If the Chamber would say 4.000 then that would encompass all the footnotes which we have had to include to try and assist the Chamber with this determination which is where the problem has really arisen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would fully satisfy --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, it would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The request is granted and the limit is set at 4.000 words. One second, please. Yes, the Chamber is informed that progress was made although perhaps not the progress which we would finally need to hear stipulations by the parties on the possible testimony of Mr. French. Is that -- when do the parties think that they could conclude their discussions on the matter because the Chamber, of course, if you do not agree on the matter, then, of course, we would have to well, at least consider our scheduling that time will be needed to call that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question actually is a little more complex because it is not only about professor French, but other witnesses that would testify about the 31 July transcript. With respect to the other witnesses, we have received from the Defence some issues that they have with that transcript. We just received that this morning, so we will review and hopefully have a final answer by the Friday hearing on -- because it will be related to scheduling in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, under Rule 94 bis we've have had a chance to review the report and assess it and we no longer require cross-examination under Rule 94 bis of Mr. French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and for the other Defence teams as I said progress has been made but whether that extends to all the Defence teams is unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We are in the same position, Your Honour, as Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the same position as well for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that -- let me just ... That professor French, that his evidence, will be introduced through an expert report and that the parties then, I take it, that there is no -- it's not contests that he qualifies as an expert because that is, of course, the first question; and then the second question whether is there any need to cross-examine him. I do understand that it is not needed. So, therefore, the expert report is ready to be decided upon as far as admission is concerned. And that for other witnesses, the situation is still unclear but that the Chamber most likely will hear by this Friday whether the parties could come to an agreement as far as the need to hear the testimony of those witnesses or the way to introduce their evidence. Is that correctly understood? Then that's clear. Then there is -- I do understand that the parties would agree that a witness statement could be tendered. Let me just check whether there is in the confidentiality there. Could we go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just verify one thing on my computer. Yes, the Chamber was informed that the further selection to be made by you, Mr. Kehoe, of the Royal Netherlands Army publication that we could expect that tomorrow or at the -- that would mean that we -- effectively we will hear about it on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If, however you could already give an indication to the registrar so that it can be -- or did you uploaded the selected portion so that we don't have to spent too much time on it. We added to that that with this proviso the Chamber is satisfied that the expert report and addendum are prima facie relevant and probative. A practical way of dealing with the matter would give a brief opportunity to make further oral submissions on the matter. Mr. Russo is here. Mr. Kehoe is here. I don't know whether the other parties would like to make submissions as well, Mr. Kuzmanovic; you are nodding yes. Mr. Cayley is nodding no, which doesn't come under the present circumstances as a surprise. I would suggest that we spend the next 15 minutes to add anything and I would say three times four minutes, first round and then second round of three times one minute. Mr. Kehoe, I think it would be appropriate that you start. Then Mr. Kuzmanovic, then Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I will be very brief and we're not certainly going to repeat the arguments that we set forth before. But I think two things are very clear at this juncture. Number one, going through an expert report, any opinions that the expert was not an expert in international humanitarian law nor an expert in law of armed conflict. So any opinions he rendered that remotely touch on either one of those issues should not be considered by the Chamber because he is not an expert in that regard. What he has given us is quite clearly what his assessment of the situation is pursuant to either doctrine or the rules of engagement for NATO and/or for the Royal Dutch Army which for his purposes is perfectly fine. It is not fine for what's to be considered by this Chamber where the standard is the laws of armed conflict. So on the first stage, anything that remotely touches the laws on -- international humanitarian law or the laws of armed conflict should not be considered his area of expertise and should not be considered by the Chamber. I think probably the more disturbing and difficult issue is the 94 bis issue, and I know Your Honours touched on this to some degree when Your Honours were talking about the addendum which is P1206 [sic] but going back to Rule 94 bis, the Prosecution was required to give us their entire expert report, and what Colonel Konings told us during the course of the cross-examination was that when his initial report was presented it was contemplated that he would provide yet another report which is the addendum. Now, without rearguing some of the items in the report, Judge, it is a very disturbing issue because the items that were set forth in his addendum go directly to targeting issues for instance and actions by our client, General Gotovina, which because of a conscious decision by the Prosecution not to provide us with that information precluded us from addressing some of those items with witnesses such as Captain Berikoff, such as Colonel Williams, such as a variety of different witnesses, individuals who were actually present at the -- present on the spot. Now, that is with all of those witnesses who talked about targets and that the Prosecution brought in here, we were prevented from cross-examining any of those individuals based on this report because they made a decision not to give it to us. Not to do it until well into the case, knowing full well, according to Colonel Konings, that when they did the first report, there was going to be a second report. Now, that frankly, Your Honour, is one of the most difficult and disturbing things when one considers what exactly transpired here because quite clearly it violates Rule 94 (a) bis, which is the specific provision. But it significantly hurt the Defence because we missed this opportunity to cross-examine based on these statements, and I can go through a list of witnesses that that applies to. So again without repeating what we did before. I don't want to do that, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Like you say, there is a new factual element in the testimony of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we now know what this witness was told that sheds an entire different light on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing I would add to that is with respect to opinions that he had regarding shelling of civilian areas outside of Knin, he had no information although he commented on the specific order he had no specific information relating to what the damage was, what the sites were, what the targets were, and in that regard, I mean, that would be the only further submission that I would have with regard to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, with respect to the qualifications to Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, I believe we covered that to some extent during the beginning of direct examination. It is clear that he has significant expertise in the use of artillery, the application of artillery in the field, the rules regarding the use of artillery, and he did give some information of his understanding of international humanitarian law. It is clear that the doctrine, as he also indicated, the doctrine which he learned and can you see from his CV in fact teaches to other members of the Royal Netherlands Army is informed by the considerations of international humanitarian law. So I don't think it is appropriate to say that anything which remotely touches on, which I'm not sure of the preciseness of that standard, anything in the report that remotely touches on international humanitarian law or the laws of armed conflict should be immediately disregarded. In any case, I think General Konings -- I'm sorry, Colonel Konings's report is quite specific in terms of what it provides to the Court and that is the first report being an understanding of the general nature of artillery, the use of artillery, and the applications of artillery in civilian-populated areas as well as his interruption as an artillery officer and as someone with significant experience in the application of artillery his interpretation of the orders in the case. The addendum clearly addresses from a military perspective the considerations that the Court needs to take into account in determining whether or not the artillery attack was illegal. That is one whether a military advantage is there to be gained from attacking a particular target given all the information and to what effect it would have on the civilian population in order to apply both the rules of proportionality and the principle of distinction. So I think his qualifications to address those have been clearly been established, so I don't think there is any reason to strike anything either in the report or from the testimony he has offered here in court over the last few days. The argument with respect to putting or the loss of the chance to put the report to other witnesses, I don't think that first of all that that bears out under the practice. In fact, the expert report which indicates his interpretation of the order of General Gotovina and several other orders including the general principles of the nature of artillery how it should be used in civilian-populated areas questions regarding those specific areas were asked of a number of fact witnesses, a number of UNMOs, a number of other UNCRO people about how you should artillery in civilian-populated areas, and General -- Colonel Konings's report was never put to him. His original expert report does address those concerns. They never asked any of the witnesses whether they would agree or disagree with those conclusions that he has come to. In any case, asking them whether they agree with Colonel Konings's assessment of the military advantage of a particular military target certainly wouldn't necessarily be relevant for this Court in terms of either evaluating the evidence of Mr. Konings or the evidence of that particular witness. So I don't think that's a valid argument to put forward in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo. Yes, I was about to invite the Prosecution also to find someone who keeps an eye on your speed of speech as is so done in the Gotovina Defence at this moment which is highly appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President. The addendum, of course, addresses the military advantage to be gained versus the risk to the civilian population of particular establishments. Now there were other witnesses in the case who testified with respect to many of those locations and again the addendum for Colonel Konings was not put to -- or the expert report was not put to any of them to address the issues the conclusions that he draws about whether artillery should or should not be used in civilian-populated areas. They were never put to those witnesses. So I think that that is in essence a red-herring argument for this Court. It doesn't really bear on the admissibility of either the expert report or the addendum. Therefore, I think his qualifications to offer the opinions which he does offer in both the expert report and in the addendum are fully supported by the qualifications which he has testified to and the answers to the questions he has given before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I respond very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may briefly respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo interestingly never addressed the issue as to why the Office of the Prosecutor violated the rule. The rule says that we were supposed to have the report. I heard no explanation as to how they violated the rule, why they violated the rule. Now for them to argue that we didn't put the first report to these witnesses is an argument that is specious at best. The article is -- that report is 99.9 percent doctrine. His addendum, and I mean Colonel Konings's addendum, 1260 is the list of items that the Colonel maintains shouldn't have been attacked in a rhetorical nature would you not think, Mr. President, that we would have asked somebody like Captain Berikoff or Colonel Williams or General Forand whether or not they considered the northern barracks as Colonel Konings put it in his report that we got in November of a low military value? An item that was the -- the headquarters for the 7th Krajina Brigade. I mean, that's just one of them. Let's say the telegraph office. No military target, don't you think, the communications that the ARSK had going through those facilities that with that information we would have asked the senior officer like General Forand whether or not that would have been something that we would have -- would have been a military target that should have been engaged? I mean that's just two. I mean, there are 30 different items. I can go down each one of them. And the fact that the Prosecution has made a decision not to give us that report, and we did not have the opportunity to ask senior military officers about all of these items, and Mr. Russo has failed to explain to this Chamber why. Why they didn't give it to us. The burden -- there is a clear violation based on what Colonel Konings said. The burden is on the Prosecutor to tell us why. And I harken back to what Mr. Russo just finished saying. He said nothing about it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kuzmanovic, anything to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo any need to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The reason I didn't address what Mr. Kehoe terms the violence of the rule is simply because there was no violation of the rule. We certainly don't agree that there was a violation of the rule. Mr. Konings seems to recall being told or mentioned to him that he would have to create an addendum at the time of the expert report. That's not the recollection of the OTP. We certainly weren't planning on springing an addendum on the Defence at the last moment. In any case, again, that argument goes to what the Defence has already argued in terms of good cause as to why addendum should not have been received into evidence. The Court, I believe, has already found in its decision there was no good cause established for why an addendum couldn't have been submitted earlier, but that nevertheless the Court decided to consider the admission or that would hear the admission of the addendum. Therefore, the issue of good cause having already been established irrespective of the OTP's disagreement as to the facts of whether or not the rule is violated, that issue has already been resolved by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if I just may intervene for one second. I think that we established that there was a new element in this -- in this debate and that is that it had been -- it was -- that the need for another report was already considered when the first report was -- was drafted. I think that's the new element, and I very much asked Mr. Kehoe to focus on new matters and we established that this was at least a new piece of information; and I haven't heard much about that because if you refer to our decision, at least that piece of information was not available to us at that moment. Not to say what consequence I'm not -- I'm inviting to you specifically address that matter as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The OTP did not intend at the time the original expert report was solicited from Colonel Konings. There was no intent to later seek an addendum. I'm not sure why Colonel Konings seems to recall a discussion of that with Mr. Tieger. In any case we did provide to the Defence at their request all communications that we had with Colonel Konings, since the beginning of his involvement with the trial team, and those in fact reflect that there was no intent to seek an addendum at the time his original report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Doesn't it then come as a surprise that as far as I remember you did not put any question to Mr. Konings on this subject in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I didn't believe that was a matter which the Court would have invited testimony on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you are now challenging the testimony of the witness in that respect without it having been put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. I certainly didn't think that it was necessary to do that. In any case, that is our position, that the communications do in fact support the OTP's position, that this wasn't discussed with him and certainly wasn't contemplated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I would like to see those communications. I received communications from the early summer, but there is no communications that we received concerning contact with Colonel Konings early on when he was developing his first report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe we provided all communications that we had with Colonel Konings. I'm not sure what else there is to provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then I suggest that apparently you are hinting at communications and the inter -- such that it gives Mr. Kehoe the impression that -- that it is communication is he not aware of, and if you would sort that out, to start with, so that we know what we're talking about and what keeps you divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I will supplement that to one degree. I do believe that the witness noted that his oral communications on this score were with Mr. Tieger. I can go back and check the transcript. But I seem to recall that is what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least he was in touch with Mr. Tieger, I would have to check that as well. Could I leave the rather factual issue of what the communications had been. We've heard from you Mr. Russo. Mr. Kehoe would like to seek verification on the basis of any recording of such communications. It doesn't seem to me to be a subject which could be fruitfully further explored at this moment in Court. If there is anything that comes up in relation to this specific issue not anything else, then the Chamber would like to be informed tomorrow, noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, tomorrow noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this then concludes the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I didn't address the remaining arguments that remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Yes, I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Also the issue about what could have been presented to earlier witnesses, first of all, whether General Forand or Mr. Berikoff or whomever what they think of Colonel Konings's opinion about the military advantage to be gained from shelling the northern barracks or any other establishment is simply not relevant. They can be asked themselves as they were what they believed the military advantage was to be gained or not gained and why. Asking one witness to offer an opinion about the validity of another' witness's evidence about that simply doesn't assist this Chamber in any way, and that would have been objected to by the OTP, in any case. I'll just slow down for the translation. And again, Your Honour, as I indicated the -- this argument that the addendum would have been put to other witnesses is clearly contradicted by the fact that the addendum was filed and given to the Defence prior to the testimony of witness 40, Kosta Novakovic, the ARSK officer who provided firsthand knowledge with respect to many of the installations which Colonel Konings addresses. They did not put the addendum to him. And he is the one to testify here who has the most direct knowledge about what the military advantage would or would not have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can respond to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm not finished I'm waiting for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let Mr. Russo first finish. The second round was one minute Mr. Russo and you were the one who took most time in the first round so would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I have nothing further to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- then unless there is something totally new. I think we started with Defence, Prosecution, Defence, Prosecution; so before I give you an opportunity, Mr. Kehoe, then first explain why it would be appropriate to give, again, an opportunity to the Defence, rather than to stick to as it is said in Latin, litis finiri oportet. There has to be an end to submission or to debate to proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I guess my first point is I just know you wanted to hear my eloquence for yet a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can play the audios as much as I want to, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is quite simple with regard to getting into objections as to what would have been allowed or not allowed. That is completely up to the Trial Chamber whether or not those things could have been confronted. What our overall position is that we were precluded from even attempting to that, and it would have been up to the Chamber as to how it would have been allowed. Mr. Russo's idea of cross-examination is quite limited in these terms because certainly throughout cross-examination, we asked Witness A based on something else that Witness B would have said and to say that the Chamber would not have been assisted by the testimony of professional officers who were there at the scene while this was taking place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do understand. Mr. Russo is thinking for us but this Chamber finally will do the thinking itself. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do have the page reference where Colonel Konings said he spoke to Mr. Tieger. It's at 14494, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Then we'll conclude for the day. I had forgotten to mention that in my estimates for Thursday and Friday, of course, also some time should be reserved for brief submissions on timing for the future. But I take it that that would not consume more than, all together, I would say 20 minutes. It's just a brief information to the Chamber. We would need so much for that, we would need so much for that, and that would not heavily influence our time scheduling for Thursday and Friday. The parties should prepare whether we do it at the beginning, Mr. Hedaraly, or at the end of Thursday and Friday's sessions, but the parties should be prepared to respond to all the outstanding issues on the -- on the pending issues list, and I take it that this will be updated, if possible, even this afternoon so that the registry can distribute all the issues which we still have to deal with. Then we adjourn for the day and we we'll resume on a Thursday, the 22nd of January, 2009, at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of January, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
